owner: W1-TRIBES. Four texts giving the six peoples of RI-LOR08 something written.
note: Every `registry` block here names a dispute registered in corpus/60-lore/data/canon-facts.json and the position the text takes. Nothing in these four settles anything, and two of them are wrong in ways their authors could not have caught. The Grange Book is the province's euphemism in an Argonian mouth on Argonian ground, which is the point of it — RI-LOR08 §5.

books.title: A Survey of the Peoples of the Interior, Made for the Provincial Office
books.author: Decius Arral, antiquarian, on a grant of the Office at Gideon
books.unreliability: A careful man measuring the wrong things, courteously, on a grant that renews on findings. He has never been more than four days inland and says so, and then generalises from four days anyway. His figure on the walkways is his own measurement and is the only number in the book he took himself.

contradicts.on: what the elevated stone walks between the stepped ruins were built for

books.text:
Are the natives of this province one people or several? It is the settled view of this Office that the province contains four native bodies with which the Empire may treat: the keepers of the wells, the compact at Gideon, the mortuary order at Soulrest, and the cutters. I have spent three years in the field on the Office's money and I am obliged to report that this is not a list of peoples. It is a list of the parties who have come to us.

The peoples are a separate matter and there are more of them than four. I have surveyed nine. I am told by every guide I have hired that nine is a low figure and that the true one cannot be given. So I record the answer I was given at the weir above Helstrom, because it is the best of them: that there are as many peoples as there are lights on the water at night, and that a man who wants a number should count the lights first and then come back.

Of the nine I can speak usefully of six.

The AGACEPHS hold the Deep Marshes and are, so far as I can judge, the most numerous. They are of many colours and their faces are long and fine. They will not chase an animal and will not eat one that was chased, which restricts their table more than a Cyrodiil would credit and does not appear to trouble them. They will not give a direction. They will, without payment and without much interest, take a lost man where he needs to go and set him down there, and I have twice owed my life to this and twice failed to buy a chart afterwards.

The PAATRU hold the Clay Moor. In the wet season they kill strangers. In the dry they trade at the moor's edge and are civil. I set this down in the plain order because the Office's abstract for last year had it as 'a hostile people' with no seasonal note, and two of the men who acted on that abstract are dead.

The SARPA of the Stone Forest have wings and use them. I have not been able to keep one in conversation for longer than an afternoon. They are the only people in the province who have seen the stepped ruins from above and they are the only people the Office has never sent a letter to.

The ARCHEIN are the estate-holders of Blackwood and they are the natives the Empire actually deals with. It is worth writing down that they consider themselves a people and not an office, and that the interior does not consider them either.

The MIREDANCERS of the Eastern Rootlands keep the tablets. I was permitted to look at the tablets and not to copy them, and I have never regretted a courtesy more.

The DEAD-WATER hold the Thornmarsh and the country north of it. Their people are of the serpentine sort. They close the tracks around Thorn when it suits them, and the Office books this as a seasonal hazard, and I have written twice to say that a hazard does not choose its months.

On the high walks between the stepped ruins I will state a finding and stand on it. They are aqueducts. I have measured eight runs with a level and a cord and each of them falls one part in four hundred along its whole length. A road does not need a fall and a builder does not put one in for pleasure. The Agacephs will tell you they are roads and point at the kerbs, and a kerb is as good a lip for water as it is for a cart. The Sarpa, I am told, claim to have roosted on them. What is a survey worth that has never questioned the only witness? I would give the whole grant to ask one properly.

On the great fall that ended the old country I have four accounts and they disagree on the number of events, on the century, and on whether there was any fire in it at all. The Office would like a date. I have written to the Office that I can give it a measurement or a date but not both, and I am waiting on the reply.

books.title: The Grange Book: Instruction for My Daughter on the Keeping of the Estate
books.author: Archein Weighs-The-Rains, of the estates east of Gideon
books.unreliability: Entirely sincere and entirely a defence. The author is an Argonian landholder explaining to her daughter how to lease Argonian labour, in careful prose, with no sense that the word is doing any work. The dangerous error is in the seventh instruction and she does not know it is there.

contradicts.on: whether a hatchling given sap from a vessel is given a soul
whether the tree behind the grange wall is a Hist or a cutting

books.text:
First. The estate is not a farm with a family attached to it. The family is the older thing and the fields were put round it, and if you ever find yourself thinking of the fields first you will make a decision you cannot take back.

Second. The tree behind the wall is ours. Your great-great-grandmother's egg was under it and mine was and yours was. The wall went up in your grandfather's time because two cutters came over in the night with a saw, and it went up over theft. It did not go up over shame and I won't have it said in this house that it did.

Third. The hatchlings are brought their sap in the copper cup, in the yard, in the morning, with the tree in sight over the wall. Do it in that order. There are people at Lilmoth who hold that this is not a hatching at all and that what we raise is borrowed. I have heard the argument made well and I have watched our own children grow up sound, and I put my own name in this book as one who was given the cup and has never in sixty years felt short of anything.

Fourth. Feed the house properly and in courses, and keep the menu written, because a written menu settles an argument before it starts.

Fifth. The labour goes out under lease and the lease is a document. Read every one. A lease that cannot be read aloud in a room with the leased party present is not a lease. And you will not sign one, whatever the season is doing to the price.

Sixth, and this is the instruction I most want you to keep. We do not deal at the quay. Not with a Dres captain, not with his mate, not on his deck, not for any money. There is a factor at Gideon and the paper is his and the money comes back through him. Your great-grandfather stood on the quay and shouted prices and every account of him begins there. The clerks will not begin an account of you there. Two generations of work went into moving us off that stone and you will not walk back onto it because a man in a hurry made it sound simple!

Seventh. When one of ours dies out of the province — and they do, at Tear, at Blackrose, at sea — you enter the death, you pay the year, and you do not send a boat after the body. Distance is nothing to a root. He is home before the letter is. I have been told otherwise by a Miredancer who was kind about it and by an Agaceph who was not, and neither of them could tell me the rate at which the thing they claim happens happens, and I asked both of them twice.

Eighth. When the interior calls you a governor, do not correct them. When the Office calls you a governor, correct them at once and in writing.

Ninth. You will be called lukiul by people whose grandparents took their names off us. Say nothing. It costs a fortune to say nothing and it is the cheapest thing you will buy all year.

Tenth. Keep this book where the daughters can reach it and not where the factors can.

books.title: The Descents: A Record Kept at the Rootpost, Lilmoth
books.author: Kept in four hands. The last hand is the Sap-Speaker's own and is not steady.
books.unreliability: A working record, not a scripture. Three of the four hands are copying a house style and the fourth has stopped bothering. The entries for the last four descents are the shortest in the book and the reader should notice what has gone out of them.

contradicts.on: whether a hatchling given sap from a vessel is given a soul
whether the great fall was one event or many

books.text:
THE FORM OF THE RECORD. On the day the Speaker goes down, her name, the hour, and the way she went — root or canopy. On the day she comes up, what she was shown. In the season after, what she made of it. Nothing else is written here, and in particular no reader's opinion, because a reader who annotates a descent has put himself in the hole.

On the giving of sap away from the tree. It is asked of us every generation and the answer has not moved. The tree must be over it. Not the sap, the tree, with the roots under it and the leaves above it, and it must see. What is given out of a vessel in a yard is not nothing. It is a loan, and the term of a loan runs out, and the running out is not our business to describe to people who have not asked.

On dying at a distance. The nearest root that is still awake takes what it can reach. It is not his tree. He goes out again in a country he has never walked and comes out a stranger to the ones who made him, and the tree that did make him is short by one in that year's count. We have the counts. This is why we keep the counts.

On the bone. The Naga-Kur carry their dead on their arms and hold that the dead go on fighting. There is nothing in a bone. But the going is delayed while the bone is above ground, and the delay is paid for at the far end by a hatchling who has not been born and cannot be consulted, and we say this plainly and we say it once, and we do not say it twice, because they are our egg-kin and they feed us when we walk north.

On the falling of the old country. Slow. The tablets we hold were begun in one hand and finished in a third, and a hand changes when a person dies. Whatever came down came down over three lives at the least. The winged people say it was one night. They have seen the ruins from above and we have not, and we have the tablets and they do not, and that is the shape the argument has had for as long as there has been one.

THE SEVENTEENTH SPEAKER. Went down at the root, fourth hour. Up on the ninth day. Shown: the tide off Archon running the wrong way and a name she would not write.

THE EIGHTEENTH SPEAKER, NEEKH-OTEI. First descent, canopy. Up on the sixth day. Shown: nothing. Sap taken: full measure.

Second descent, root. Up on the fourth day. Shown: nothing.

Third descent, root. Up on the third day. Shown: nothing. The gold has come into the mouth.

Fourth descent, root. Up on the second day and up by herself, which the form does not have a line for. Shown: nothing. Bark has come into both arms.

Fifth descent to be entered.

books.title: Told at the Weir: Notes of a Factor Who Went To Buy a Chart
books.author: Ranaso Quick-Tally, under-factor of the Wet Ledger, Gideon
books.unreliability: A lukiul factor writing down what interior Argonians told him while entirely failing at the errand he was sent on. He records the sayings accurately and draws the wrong conclusion from most of them, and the entry for the eleventh day is the one to read twice.

contradicts.on: whether the tree behind the grange wall is a Hist or a cutting
what the elevated stone walks between the stepped ruins were built for

books.text:
SENT: to obtain from the Agacephs of the Deep Marshes a chart of the interior water, at a price to be agreed. Thirty years the house has been at this. I am the ninth under-factor to be sent and the first to be sent with an Argonian face, and the house thinks this will make the difference.

DAY ONE. Arrived at the weir. Fed at once, without being asked who I was. Fish out of a fixed trap, rootmat, a bitter yellow fruit that made my jaw ache. They did not ask my errand.

DAY TWO. Asked about the chart. Was taken instead to see a bank of the river I had asked about, and set down on it, and brought back. Asked again. Was told: we will take you.

DAY THREE. Understood that this is the whole of it. So they will carry you to the place. They will not tell you the place. A chart is a direction and they do not give directions, and thirty years of dinners have gone into finding this out.

DAY FOUR. On the grange tree at Gideon, unprompted, from the weir-keeper. She says it is a cutting. She says a man carried it off the Rootlands in a wet sack in the old time and put it in a hole and built a wall round the hole, and that it grows and drinks and holds nothing. She says taste the water under it: theirs runs clear and clear means the root is going sideways after something. I have drunk that water at the grange all my life. It's clear! And I haven't slept well since.

DAY SIX. On the high walks in the stone country. They say roads, and they say it the way a man says a thing he has never had to defend. Door to door, kerbs, steps at both ends. When I said the Imperial had measured a fall in them, the guide said: what is a fall? And when I explained it she said that water also goes door to door.

DAY EIGHT. On dying away from the tree. Distance costs, they say, and what comes back comes back short. I asked how short. Not one of them at this weir will put a number on it and I have now asked four. They're perfectly willing to say the thing and perfectly unwilling to measure it, and I don't think this is evasion. I think there is no unit.

DAY ELEVEN. My grandmother was under lease at Blackrose for six years and came out and had me. I have written the sentence above and I'm going to leave it in the book, and I'm not going to explain to the house why it sits in a report about a chart.

DAY TWELVE. Offered them money in front of the whole weir, which I now understand was a rudeness of a kind I cannot repair. The eldest said: we will take you anywhere, this week or in ten years, and you may bring the house, and we will feed you and bring you back. Then she asked: have you eaten?

RETURNED. No chart. Recommend the house stop sending under-factors and start sending people who want to go somewhere.
